Please read this carefully:

<document>
# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

</document>
response:
I've read it closely. This is a good follow-up. It does what the earlier documents asked for:
- registers the mediation test before the outcome data exist;
- adds a second, independent hours measure;
- reports the counter arm's failure plainly;
- labels the Halden survivors as an upper bound;
- corrects both the "entirely an artifact" and "no decay" claims with evidence rather than rhetoric.

I checked the arithmetic and it holds:
- 0.966 / 0.88 gives +9.8%, and 0.966 / 0.89 gives +8.5%.
- 96.8 / 86.6 gives +11.8%.
- The mediation shares sum to 100%.
- The counter-arm staffing estimate is consistent with the nine-month figures: 0.83 × 1.067 ≈ 0.886, so about 13% more staff would be needed to restore throughput.

There are still some significant issues. The first is new and could change how the decline is read.

## 1. The control offices' meeting audit may explain part of the "decline"

- Two of the seven control case-processing offices cut meetings at month 15 and gained about 4% in output per hour. That is contamination of the control arm. "On their own initiative" in a county running a well-publicised trial about meetings and hours is exactly how spillover happens.
- Improving the control arm shrinks the measured treatment effect. If two of seven control offices gained around 4% from month 15, the control average rises by roughly 1.2 points for that period. That is a meaningful share of the 2.7-point fall from 12.5% to 9.8%.
- The report treats the audit only as a hint that gains might be available without cutting hours. It doesn't consider its effect on the main estimate.
- The authors should report:
  - treated and control trajectories separately, so readers can see whether treated offices faded or control offices improved;
  - a sensitivity analysis excluding the two audit offices, or ending at month 14.
- Until then, "consistent with some fading of an initial effect" is only one of two explanations.

## 2. The mediation result is better than before, but "confirms" is too strong

- **Overlap with the data that generated the hypothesis.** The meetings hypothesis came from months 1–9. If the 24-month mediation model includes those months, part of the "confirmation" re-uses the exploratory data. Pre-registration at month 11 guards against choosing the model after seeing results. It doesn't make old data independent. A test restricted to months 10–24 would be a cleaner confirmation.
- **The effective sample is 14 offices, not office-months.** The treatment-to-mediator path varies only at office level, with 7 v 7. "A larger sample of office-months" adds precision only within offices. An interval of 28–66% looks narrow for 14 clusters, and the few-cluster inference problem I raised at nine months still applies.
- **Does log-in time include meetings?** This decides what the meetings result means.
  - If meetings fall *outside* log-in time, cutting them doesn't mechanically raise output per log-hour. The meetings pathway would then reflect something substantive, such as fewer interruptions and longer focus blocks.
  - If meetings fall *inside*, part of the 47% is arithmetic: time that produced no recorded output was removed from the denominator.
  - Either finding is useful, but they mean different things.
- **Shares of a correlated pair.** Fewer meetings plausibly reduce fatigue, so the mediators aren't independent. The report should say whether they were estimated jointly and how shared variance was allocated.
- The limitations section rightly notes the no-unmeasured-confounding assumption. The Summary's "confirms" should be "supports."

## 3. The Summary mixes measures

- "Fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months" compares a timesheet estimate with a log-based one.
- The like-for-like comparison is 12.5% to 9.8%, a fall of about 22%. The body gets this right. The Summary should too.
- The intervals overlap heavily (6.9–18.4 against 4.6–15.2). The decline is plausible but not statistically established, before even considering the contamination in §1.
- Two time points can't show whether the gain has levelled off or is still falling. "Declined but not disappeared" is fair. Nothing yet supports "stable at about 9%."

## 4. Few-cluster inference is still unaddressed

- The nine-month report used conventional clustered standard errors with 7 v 7 offices. The follow-up appears to do the same.
- "Excludes zero by a clear margin" (lower bound 3.4%) should be checked with wild cluster bootstrap or randomisation inference. With 14 offices, randomisation inference is exact.
- The result may well survive, but the paper's central claim against the re-analysis rests on this interval.

## 5. Backlog and deadline data are still missing

- The nine-month report named backlog growth beyond statutory deadlines as a risk. At 24 months it's measurable and still not reported.
- Output here is cases *closed*. A backlog that grows, ages or tilts toward hard cases would flatter the per-hour figures.
- The appeal-overturn rate (3.2% v 3.0%) now has enough time to mature, which is good, but it still lacks a confidence interval.

## 6. "Stricter" hours measure

- Log-in time is a different construct from timesheets, not necessarily a stricter one:
  - it counts idle time while logged in;
  - it misses off-system work (phone calls, paper files, possibly meetings);
  - it misses work done on the day off outside the system.
- The log figure is valuable as a second measure, and the fact that the two agree (−11% v −12%) is reassuring. But it isn't clearly closer to "work actually done."
- Also confirm that logs were available for the pre-period. The difference-in-differences estimate needs a baseline, and the measure was "added" at follow-up.

## 7. The Halden subset

- **Non-response.** Of 23 organisations with records, 14 responded. Organisations that reverted or did badly may be less likely to respond, so the 3-of-14 reversion rate and the 11.8% gain are both likely flattering. The authors call the estimate an upper bound, but non-response deserves its own mention.
- **Baseline mismatch.** The −13.4% uses 40.3 hours as baseline, which is the 27-organisation figure from the re-analysis. The 11 continuing organisations need their own baseline. Also confirm that all 11 have time-tracking data; only 17 of the 23 did.
- **The marketing agency.** It reverted citing client deadlines. The Summary groups it under "client-facing or coverage obligations," but marketing was coded as discretionary in the pilot. Tight client deadlines are a third kind of constraint that the discretionary/coverage split doesn't capture, and this case deserves a sentence.
- **Conflict of interest.** R. Okafor is an author of the original Halden paper, which the re-analysis showed had misreported attrition. Section 4 is candid, but the involvement should be stated explicitly.

## 8. §5, on the earlier claims, is fair

- **On the re-analysis:** it credits the measurement critique and rejects only the "entirely an artifact" conclusion. That is the right line. One concession is missing: the re-analysis's novelty concern was partly borne out, since the gain did decline.
- **On the meta-analysis:** the supplementary table showing all four long studies were uncontrolled and used scheduled hours confirms the concern. It is a decisive rebuttal of "novelty can be set aside."
- But "the one controlled study with long follow-up" is this one, with seven treated offices and a possibly contaminated control arm. It shows decline is *possible*. It can't establish the size or pattern of decline in general.

## Where the evidence now stands, across all five documents

- **Discretionary work (case-processing, back office):** a gain in output per actual hour of roughly 8–10% in the best evidence. It is smaller than headline pilots, declined somewhat over two years, and is roughly half attributable to cutting meetings. Output per worker sits a few percent below control. The hours cut is mostly, not fully, paid for.
- **Coverage-bound work:** service worsens. Restoring it costs roughly 9–13% more. The one randomised arm was ended.
- **Open questions:**
  - whether the gain stabilises after 24 months;
  - how much of it needs the hours cut at all, as opposed to the reorganisation the cut prompts (no study has a "reorganise only" arm);
  - whether a single public employer generalises.

The most useful next study would randomise three arms: reduced hours, meeting and workflow reorganisation without reduced hours, and control. It should have enough clusters for valid inference and measure backlog alongside throughput.

I can draft this as a referee report, or write the cross-document synthesis as a standalone brief.
